analysis.one_liner: Caps monthly steel imports at their past average volume using quotas and tariff surcharges.
analysis.headline: A steel import quota bill with 210 House cosponsors — 166 Democrats, 43 Republicans, and 1 Independent — never got a committee or floor vote and died when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the President, within 60 days, to hold total steel imports to the average monthly tonnage imported during the 36 months before July 1997 — using import quotas, tariff surcharges, or negotiated export limits with foreign suppliers. Customs would have been authorized to turn away steel shipments above the allowed levels, and the restraints would have lasted three years. It applied to a broad list of products: finished steel, semifinished steel, iron ore, and coke.
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic steelmakers and the roughly unionized workforce in steel towns — Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana, West Virginia — would gain protected sales volumes and steadier jobs, since imports could never exceed the pre-crisis baseline no matter how much cheaper foreign steel was. Communities built around mills, coke ovens, and iron ore mines would share the benefit.

how_it_helps.text: Caps total monthly steel imports at the average monthly tonnage of the 36 months before July 1997, using quotas, tariff surcharges, or negotiated voluntary export restraint agreements, so foreign competition cannot push past that floor.
Authorizes the Customs Service to refuse entry to any steel products exceeding the allowed levels, and directs Treasury and Commerce to build an enforcement program within 60 days of enactment.
Covers a broad product list — semifinished steel, plates, sheets, bars, pipe and tube, iron ore, and coke — measured by tonnage, and runs for three years.

analysis.who_pays: Steel-consuming manufacturers — autos, appliances, construction, machinery — and ultimately their customers would pay more, because the supply of cheaper imported steel would be capped regardless of demand. Foreign steel producers and importers would lose market access, and the government would take on the cost and legal exposure of policing a quota regime that likely conflicts with world trade rules.

drawbacks.text: A hard tonnage cap ignores economic growth and market shifts: demand for steel could rise above the 1994–1997 average, forcing domestic buyers onto a tighter, pricier supply.

Quotas raise steel prices for every manufacturer that buys steel, a cost that flows through to consumers of cars, appliances, and construction — a diffuse hit spread across the whole economy to protect one region's jobs.
A unilateral quota regime negotiated in 60 days would likely run against United States trade commitments and invite retaliation against American exports.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a concentrated, visible benefit — protected steel jobs in a hard-hit region — for a diffuse, real cost: higher steel prices for manufacturers and consumers nationwide, plus trade-rule friction. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how badly one weighs the laid-off steelworker against the slightly higher car or appliance price; the design, a rigid tonnage freeze at a past baseline, is blunt even by the standards of its supporters' own quota proposals.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means Committee and then its Trade Subcommittee for nearly two years with no markup, hearing, or floor vote, and expired when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Introduced February 2, 1999 by Rep. Peter Visclosky with roughly 100 original cosponsors — including the Democratic Leader Dick Gephardt and members from both parties from steel-producing states.
It reached a total of 210 cosponsors: 166 of 211 House Democrats, 43 of 223 Republicans, and the chamber's lone Independent.
The House referred it to Ways and Means on the day of introduction, and to the Subcommittee on Trade on February 9, 1999; the action record shows no further movement of any kind.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Steel-importing manufacturers and consumers kept unrestricted access to cheaper foreign steel; steelworkers and steel towns got no quota relief. The committee with jurisdiction avoided a politically difficult vote on a bill most of the House nominally supported.

for.name: Peter J. Visclosky
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-IN), bill sponsor from a Northwest Indiana steel district
for.what_they_did: Introduced the quota bill and recruited original cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: Dick Gephardt
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor at introduction.

for.name: United Steelworkers
for.what_they_did: Campaigning for import relief during the late-1990s steel import surge and layoffs, the union publicly backed quota legislation like this bill.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tariffs and trade, chaired by Rep. Bill Archer (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Trade Subcommittee on February 9, 1999 and took no further action — no markup, no hearing vote, no release to the floor — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Subcommittee on Trade
against.role: Ways and Means trade subcommittee, chaired by Rep. Philip Crane (R-IL)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from referral onward; the record shows no action it took on H.R. 506.

against.name: Clinton administration
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory import quotas, arguing instead for anti-dumping cases and other relief channels during the steel import surge.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan but skewed Democratic: 166 of 211 Democrats signed on versus 43 of 223 Republicans, and the bill still died in a Republican-controlled committee without a vote.

industries.industry: Domestic steelmakers (mills, iron ore, and coke producers)
industries.note: The quota would lock in sales volumes and support prices and employment for an industry and its unionized workforce. But the mechanism is a supply cap: steel users and consumers pay more so that steel producers earn more.
Import relief would protect high-wage steel jobs in mill towns, the reason the bill drew cosponsorship from both parties across steel-producing states.
Capping imports means paying more for a core input, costs that pass through to their customers. Their interest in plentiful cheap steel runs with consumers' interest.
Customs would be authorized to turn their shipments away at the border once quotas filled, ending access to the US market for anything above the frozen baseline.
